chunks: Inductor impedance equation. The question: What is the equation for impedance of an inductor?
The impedance of an ideal inductor is Z equals j omega L , where omega equals 2 pi f . Its size grows in proportion to frequency.
At DC it is zero, so the inductor is a plain wire. At very high frequency it is huge.
The j means the voltage leads the current by 90°, and that on average the inductor stores and returns energy without wasting any.
Imagine rocking a heavy wheel back and forth. A slow rock takes little effort because the wheel can follow.
A fast rock takes a lot of effort, because the wheel's inertia fights every reversal. The faster the rocking, the harder you work.
An inductor behaves the same way with current: the faster the current changes sign, the more voltage it takes. The picture does not show the 90° timing offset.
The voltage is proportional to the slope of the current, so it peaks where the current crosses zero (steepest) and is zero where the current peaks (flat).
That's the 90° lead, a quarter period (2. 5 microseconds at 100 kilohertz).
Impedance (Z): the AC opposition to current, in ohms. Reactance ( X L equals omega L ): the part of impedance that grows with frequency in an inductor.
omega (omega): angular frequency, equal to 2 pi f . Phase (+90°): the voltage peaks a quarter cycle before the current. Inductor equation: v equals L di over dt .
Take a 10 microhenries inductor. At 1 megahertz, the impedance size is 2 pi times 10 to the 6 times 10 times 10 to the -6 , which is about 63 ohms. At 100 kilohertz it is about 6.
3 ohms. Ten times lower frequency gives ten times lower impedance. That is the whole idea.
"An ideal inductor's impedance is Z L equals j omega L equals j2 pi fL . It comes from v equals L di over dt : for a sinusoid, the derivative multiplies by j omega .
The magnitude omega L rises linearly with frequency, so it's a short at DC and an open at very high frequency, and the j means voltage leads current by 90° with no power dissipated.
For example, 10 microhenries at 1 megahertz is about 63 ohms. In Laplace terms it's sL ."
